The Iron Horse & Fleet Archive

Engineered for Autonomy // Driven by Family // Firewalled by Law

Corporate Provenance: The 2004–2015 Diversification

When The Stardust Engine commissioned their 2002 Sainte-Claire 45H3 and 2004 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30, both coaches were originally purchased cash-in-full by Engine Room Records, LLC—which at the time served as the family's single all-purpose operating company.

After the band signed off at the conclusion of 2004's Progress Street to recover from severe touring burnout, CEO Holly O'Connell spent the 2004–2015 hiatus systematically unbundling the label into a fortress of specialized entities. Realizing that a single highway accident involving a 45,000-pound motorcoach could expose the band's master recordings to catastrophic litigation, Holly spun off the physical properties and heavy fleet into Stardust Strategic Assets, LLC (a subsidiary of Stardust Properties, LLC), completing the anonymous corporate web in the 2015 Delaware Migration.

INTERSTATE FLAGSHIP 2002 Sainte-Claire 45H3 — "The Iron Horse"
ORIGIN: SAINTE-CLAIRE, QUÉBEC

The Interstate Fortress (60-Inch Vertical Hydraulic Lift)

Commissioned on March 14, 2002, during the band's sold-out Trans-Canada Tour in Montréal, "The Iron Horse" is a ground-up custom 45-foot high-deck tri-axle entertainer coach built by Sainte-Claire Coachworks in Québec.

Because a high-deck interstate cruiser places the main living floor 60 inches above the pavement to accommodate massive underfloor luggage and equipment bays, Ryan O'Connell could not board via a conventional ramp. Holly O'Connell presented the Québécois engineering team—in flawless French—with structural schematics for a 400-pound commercial hydraulic cassette platform lift integrated directly into a full-height mid-ship accessibility door.

Impressed by the family's humility and engineering rigor (and disgusted by an American pop star demanding a rooftop Jacuzzi that compromised frame rigidity), Sainte-Claire's VP of Sales moved The Stardust Engine to Bay 1. Wrapped in the band's signature Cosmic Nebula violet, cyan, and amber stardust livery over Obsidian Midnight paint, The Iron Horse gave Ryan total autonomy across North America's interstates.

The Low-Floor Blacksburg Cruiser (Kneeling Curb Ramp)

While the 45-foot Sainte-Claire 45H3 was built to cross continents, maneuvering a towering tri-axle highway liner down tight residential streets like Progress Street NE or through the campus turns of Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI)—and waiting several minutes to deploy a heavy 60-inch vertical hydraulic lift for a quick local trip—was impractical.

In early 2004, while recording their homecoming album Progress Street, The Stardust Engine became the very first launch customer for Prairie Coachworks' newly restyled 30-foot low-floor platform: the 2004 RLFD30 (Restyled Low-Floor Diesel, 30-Foot).

Built as a single-door executive day-coach (deleting the rear transit exit door in favor of continuous dark-tinted acoustic lounge glass), the RLFD30 uses pneumatic kneeling suspension and a simple front flip-out aluminum ADA ramp. Inspired by the family's fond memories of riding Blue Ridge Transit's Route 1 along Main Street and Progress Street during their CPI student years, Ryan can roll straight off the Blacksburg sidewalk and into the cabin in five seconds flat.

LAUNCH CUSTOMER CERTIFICATE #001

Archivist's Note: Of all the vehicles in the family fleet, the 2004 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30 holds a uniquely personal place in the band's heart. Because The Stardust Engine signed on as the official Launch Customer (Serial #001) for Prairie Coachworks' restyled 30-foot low-floor platform before the first municipal transit orders were even delivered, the manufacturer issued the following press release on Delivery Day. Ryan, Cassidy, Holly, Evan, and Tyler keep a framed copy mounted on the forward bulkhead just behind the driver's cockpit—and carry laminated copies in the glovebox to show fellow transit enthusiasts on the road.

FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE — MAY 18, 2004 PRAIRIE COACHWORKS, INC. // SPECIALTY & EXECUTIVE TRANSIT DIVISION

PRAIRIE COACHWORKS UNVEILS RESTYLED 2004 RLFD30 LOW-FLOOR PLATFORM; DELIVERS SERIAL #001 LAUNCH COACH TO INDEPENDENT ROCK ACT "THE STARDUST ENGINE"

First-of-its-kind 30-foot Restyled Low-Floor Diesel (RLFD30) single-door executive coach pairs heavy-duty urban transit accessibility with custom acoustic touring architecture for Blacksburg, Virginia musicians.

WINNIPEG, MB & BLACKSBURG, VA (May 18, 2004) — Prairie Coachworks, Inc. today announced the official commercial launch and first customer delivery of its all-new 2004 RLFD30 (Restyled Low-Floor Diesel, 30-Foot) heavy-duty coach platform. In an industry first, Serial #001 of the restyled low-floor line has been delivered not to a metropolitan transit authority, but to Virginia-based independent rock band The Stardust Engine and their operating label, Engine Room Records, LLC, who serve as the global Launch Customer for the RLFD30 program.

Engineered on Prairie Coachworks' newly restyled aerodynamic front and rear fiberglass masks with roof-integrated HVAC fairings, the 30-foot rigid monocoque chassis was developed for tight university corridors and historic downtown street grids where 40-foot and 60-foot coaches cannot easily maneuver. Working directly with Engine Room Records Chief Executive Officer Holly O'Connell, Prairie Coachworks' Specialty Vehicles Engineering Group created a bespoke Front-Door-Only Executive Configuration—deleting the standard rear exit door to form a continuous, studio-insulated acoustic lounge with flush-mounted frameless dark-tinted panoramic glass.

At the core of Serial #001's mission is uncompromising, zero-delay accessibility for frontman and lead guitarist Ryan O'Connell, who has used a manual wheelchair since surviving a 1990 highway collision. By combining Prairie Coachworks' fast-acting pneumatic front-axle kneeling suspension with an integrated heavy-gauge aluminum flip-out ADA boarding ramp, the RLFD30 lowers its entrance threshold directly to the sidewalk curb—allowing O'Connell to roll from pavement to cabin unassisted in under five seconds.

"When Holly and Ryan O'Connell approached us with their specifications, they didn't ask for rock-star vanity—they asked for transit-grade reliability, structural integrity, and five-second curb autonomy on the streets of Blacksburg. Having a band of former Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute commuters christen Serial #001 of the RLFD30—complete with factory-programmed Luminator Horizon amber LED headsigns reading PROGRESS STREET and THE STARDUST ENGINE—is the proudest launch in our division's history."

Marc-André Beaulieu, Vice President of Engineering & Specialty Coaches, Prairie Coachworks, Inc.

In another milestone for the Winnipeg delivery center, The Stardust Engine became the first private customer in Prairie Coachworks history to dispatch three of its own principals—CEO Holly O'Connell, bassist Evan Wright, and drummer Tyler Wright—all holding valid Class A Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDL) with full Passenger (P) and Airbrake endorsements, to personally execute the factory road-test inspection and pilot Serial #001 home to Montgomery County, Virginia.

"In college, riding the low-floor campus buses down Main Street and Progress Street was how my sisters, my cousins, and I got our independence back after the crash. Being the launch customer for the 2004 RLFD30 means that wherever we pull up to the curb, the ramp flips out in five seconds and we're home. We're prouder of this 30-foot bus than any platinum plaque on the wall."

Ryan O'Connell, Lead Vocalist & Guitarist, The Stardust Engine
### END RELEASE // PRAIRIE COACHWORKS ARCHIVE SERIAL #2004-RLFD30-001 ###
Post-1990 Security & Safety Mandate

The CDL Protocol: Why No Outsider Ever Drives the Bus

Following the December 10, 1990 crash on Interstate 81 that left Ryan O'Connell with a complete T10 spinal cord injury, the family instituted an unbreakable operational rule: no hired commercial driver would ever hold their lives in their hands again.

Before taking delivery of heavy coaches, Holly O'Connell, Evan Wright, and Tyler Wright all completed commercial heavy-vehicle training and earned their Class A Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDL) with full Passenger (P) and Airbrake endorsements. Whether piloting the 45-foot Sainte-Claire 45H3 across Canada or kneeling the 30-foot Prairie Coachworks RLFD30 at the curb on Progress Street NE, a member of the family is always in the driver's seat.

Authorized CDL Operators
  • Tyler Wright: Class A CDL (P, Airbrake) — Primary Interstate Operator
  • Evan Wright: Class A CDL (P, Airbrake) — Co-Captain / Night Shift
  • Holly O'Connell: Class A CDL (P, Airbrake) — Relief & Tactical Operator
